moldavian-democratic-republic.t: Short-lived republic of Bessarabia proclaimed after the Russian Revolution, which voted for union with Romania in 1918.
moldavian-democratic-republic.o: After the fall of the Russian monarchy in 1917, Bessarabia's Romanian-speaking majority organised politically. A regional council, the Sfatul Țării, met in Chișinău and on 2 December 1917 proclaimed the Moldavian Democratic Republic as an autonomous member of a planned Russian federation, with Ion Inculeț as president.
moldavian-democratic-republic.r: The council, elected by soldiers' congresses, peasants and national groups, struggled to govern amid deserting soldiers, peasant land seizures and Bolshevik agitation. In January 1918 Romanian troops entered Bessarabia, invited by part of the leadership, and drove out Bolshevik units. The republic proclaimed full independence on 24 January 1918, and land reform was a central issue.
moldavian-democratic-republic.e: On 27 March 1918 the Sfatul Țării voted for union with the Kingdom of Romania, under Romanian military presence. Soviet Russia never recognised the union, and the Soviet Union annexed Bessarabia in 1940; much of it is now Moldova.

maedi.t: Thracian tribe of the middle Strymon valley that raided Macedon for centuries and fought Philip II, Alexander and Rome.
maedi.o: The Maedi lived along the middle Strymon (Struma) in modern south-western Bulgaria from at least the 5th century BCE, when Thucydides mentions them as independent Thracian highlanders.
maedi.r: Known mainly from Greek and Roman accounts of war, the Maedi were a tribal people of hill country, often raiding Macedonia. In 340 BCE the young Alexander, regent for Philip II, defeated them and founded Alexandroupolis in their land. Some later writers held that Spartacus was a Maedian.
maedi.e: After Macedon became a Roman province in 146 BCE, the Maedi raided it repeatedly; Roman commanders including Sulla fought them in the 80s BCE. They were later absorbed into the Roman province of Thrace.

malaka.t: A Phoenician harbour on the Costa del Sol that grew into Málaga, one of Iberia's oldest cities.
malaka.o: Phoenicians settled the bay of Málaga in the 8th century BCE, first at Cerro del Villar on an island in the mouth of the Guadalhorce, and then on the hill below the later Alcazaba, where Malaka grew into the main settlement by the 6th century BCE.
malaka.r: Malaka traded with the Iberian peoples of the interior and lived from fishing, fish salting and crafts. It was later drawn into the Carthaginian sphere, and its coins with Punic legends showed a smith god with tongs. Strabo described it as a market for the nomads of the opposite African coast.
malaka.e: After 206 BCE Malaka came under Rome as an allied city. As Malaca it received municipal status under the Flavian emperors, recorded in the bronze Lex Flavia Malacitana, and continued as a major port of Hispania Baetica.

mirdasid-emirate.t: A Bedouin dynasty of the Banu Kilab that ruled Aleppo for half a century, balancing between Byzantium and the Fatimids.
mirdasid-emirate.o: Salih ibn Mirdas, chief of the Banu Kilab who dominated the steppe of northern Syria, joined the 1024 Bedouin alliance against the Fatimids and captured Aleppo from its Fatimid governor, becoming its emir.
mirdasid-emirate.r: Salih was killed in 1029 at al-Uqhuwana, but his son Shibl al-Dawla Nasr defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos III near Azaz in 1030 and then accepted Byzantine protection. The Mirdasids relied on tribal horsemen and the city's Shi'i notables, alternated between Fatimid and Byzantine alliances, and under Thimal ruled a wide area of northern Syria. Family quarrels repeatedly divided the emirate.
mirdasid-emirate.e: In 1070 Mahmud ibn Nasr switched allegiance to the Abbasid caliph to placate the Seljuks. Weakened by internal feuds and Turkmen pressure, the dynasty lost Aleppo in 1080 to the Uqaylid Muslim ibn Quraysh, and the city soon passed to the Seljuk Sultanate of Syria.

melos.t: Dorian island of the Cyclades whose refusal to join Athens ended in the massacre of 416 BCE described in Thucydides's Melian Dialogue.
melos.o: Melos was famous from the Neolithic for its obsidian and had an important Bronze Age town at Phylakopi. In the early Iron Age it was settled by Dorians who claimed Spartan descent. The city grew on the bay of Klima, on the north side of the island's great natural harbour.
melos.r: Melos was a small oligarchic state that sent ships to Salamis in 480 BCE but stayed outside the Delian League as the only Dorian island in the Cyclades. Athens attacked it in 426 BCE and besieged it in 416 BCE. Thucydides's Melian Dialogue presents the debate over power and justice before the siege.
melos.e: After the city surrendered in 416 BCE, Athens killed the men, enslaved the women and children and settled 500 colonists. Lysander restored surviving Melians in 405 BCE. The later town produced the Aphrodite of Milos, the Venus de Milo.

manteno-huancavilca.t: Seafaring chiefdoms of the Ecuadorian coast whose balsa rafts carried spondylus shell and trade goods along the Pacific from Mexico to Peru.
manteno-huancavilca.o: The Manteño and Huancavilca peoples developed from earlier coastal traditions in present-day Manabí, Guayas and Santa Elena from around 800. The Manteño occupied the central coast, with Jocay, near modern Manta, as a main port, while the Huancavilca lived to the south around the Gulf of Guayaquil.
manteno-huancavilca.r: The coastal chiefdoms formed a league of lordships under several chiefs. They were skilled sailors: in 1526 the Spanish pilot Bartolomé Ruiz met a large sailing balsa raft loaded with trade goods off the coast. Spondylus shell, prized in Andean ritual, was a key export. The Manteño carved U-shaped stone seats and stelae, and built settlements with stone foundations on hills such as Cerro de Hojas-Jaboncillo.
manteno-huancavilca.e: The coastal peoples largely avoided Inca rule. Spanish conquest after 1534, followed by epidemics, devastated the population, and Portoviejo and Guayaquil were founded in their lands. Descendant communities on the Santa Elena peninsula have revived Manteño and Huancavilca identity.

munqidhite-emirate-of-shaizar.t: A small Arab emirate on the Orontes that survived between Crusaders and Muslim powers and produced the memoirist Usama ibn Munqidh.
munqidhite-emirate-of-shaizar.o: The Banu Munqidh, an Arab family of the Kinana, held lands near Shaizar on the Orontes. In 1081 Ali ibn Munqidh acquired the fortress of Shaizar from its Byzantine-appointed bishop and made it the seat of a family emirate.
munqidhite-emirate-of-shaizar.r: Shaizar's castle on a ridge above the Orontes was its strength. The emirs paid tribute or fought as needed against the Principality of Antioch, the Nizari Ismailis and Turkish rulers of Aleppo, and withstood a siege by the Byzantine emperor John II Komnenos and Frankish allies in 1138. Usama ibn Munqidh, born there in 1095, wrote the Kitab al-I'tibar, vivid memoirs of hunting, war and Frankish customs.
munqidhite-emirate-of-shaizar.e: In 1157 a great earthquake destroyed the citadel during a family celebration and killed nearly all the Munqidhites. Nur al-Din of the Zengid dynasty took the ruins and rebuilt the fortress.

monastic-community-of-mount-athos.t: Self-governing Orthodox monastic republic on the Athos peninsula in northern Greece, continuously inhabited by monks for over a thousand years.
monastic-community-of-mount-athos.o: Hermits lived on the mountainous Athos peninsula from at least the 9th century. In 963 Athanasios the Athonite, with the backing of his friend the general and future emperor Nikephoros Phokas, founded the Great Lavra, the first large monastery. The first charter, the Tragos, issued under John Tzimiskes around 972, organised the community under a Protos at Karyes.
monastic-community-of-mount-athos.r: Twenty ruling monasteries, Greek, Serbian (Hilandar), Russian (Saint Panteleimon), Bulgarian (Zograf) and others, own the land and send representatives to the Holy Community at Karyes. Women have been excluded since the Middle Ages. Life follows the Byzantine liturgical calendar and day, and the monasteries hold great libraries of manuscripts and icons.
monastic-community-of-mount-athos.e: Athos kept its autonomy under Byzantine, Serbian and Ottoman rulers. Greek forces took it in 1912, and the Treaty of Lausanne and the Greek constitution of 1927 confirmed its self-government under Greek sovereignty, with a civil governor. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

metsepole.t: Livonian coastal district north of Riga, known from Henry of Livonia's chronicle and absorbed by the Archbishopric of Riga.
metsepole.o: Metsepole, whose name means 'forest land', was a district of the Finnic-speaking Livonians along the Gulf of Riga north of the Gauja, around modern Limbaži. It appears in the chronicle of the Livonian crusade in the early 13th century.
metsepole.r: Its people lived from farming, fishing and coastal trade, led by local elders. Little else is recorded beyond their part in the wars and baptisms of the period.
metsepole.e: The Livs of Metsepole submitted to Bishop Albert and accepted baptism around 1206, after the failure of a Liv revolt. The area became part of the Archbishopric of Riga and Terra Mariana, and the Livonian population merged gradually into the Latvians.

margraviate-of-baden.t: A south-west German margraviate on the upper Rhine, divided for two centuries, reunited in 1771 and later the Grand Duchy of Baden.
margraviate-of-baden.o: Hermann II, of the Zähringen family, first called himself margrave of Baden in 1112, after the castle of Baden near Baden-Baden. The title derived from his family's claim to the March of Verona. The margraves built lands in the upper Rhine plain and the northern Black Forest.
margraviate-of-baden.r: In 1535 Baden split into Catholic Baden-Baden and Protestant Baden-Durlach. Louis William of Baden-Baden, the 'Turkish Louis', fought the Ottomans and built Rastatt Palace. Charles III William of Baden-Durlach founded Karlsruhe in 1715, a planned city radiating from the palace. Charles Frederick, an enlightened ruler, abolished serfdom in 1783.
margraviate-of-baden.e: The two lines reunited under Charles Frederick in 1771. Napoleon's reorganisation tripled Baden's size: it became an electorate in 1803 and a grand duchy in 1806. Today it forms part of Baden-Württemberg.

megara-hyblaea.t: Greek colony on Sicily's east coast whose excavated remains are a key source for early Greek town planning, destroyed by Gelon of Syracuse in 483 BCE.
megara-hyblaea.o: Settlers from Megara in Greece, after failed attempts elsewhere, were offered land by the Sicel king Hyblon and founded Megara Hyblaea around 728 BCE, on the coast north of Syracuse. The name honoured both their mother city and their native host.
megara-hyblaea.r: Excavations by French archaeologists have shown that the town was laid out with regular streets and house plots soon after its foundation, among the earliest planned Greek settlements known. An agora with temples and stoas developed in the 7th century BCE. Its territory was limited by Syracuse and Leontini, so around 628 BCE it founded the more distant colony of Selinous in western Sicily.
megara-hyblaea.e: Gelon of Syracuse captured Megara Hyblaea in 483 BCE, moved its wealthy citizens to Syracuse and sold the common people into slavery. A smaller town was refounded in the time of Timoleon in the 340s BCE and destroyed again by the Romans in 214 BCE.

myus.t: The smallest of the twelve Ionian cities, near the mouth of the Maeander, eventually abandoned as silt turned its harbour into marsh.
myus.o: Myus was founded, by tradition, by Cydrelus, a son of Codrus of Athens, c. 1000 BCE on the Latmian Gulf near the mouth of the Maeander. Though small, it ranked as one of the twelve members of the Ionian League.
myus.r: Myus lived from fishing and the farmland of the Maeander valley. It sent three ships to the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE. Later the Persian king Artaxerxes I granted the exiled Themistocles the revenues of Myus to supply him with relish. It then paid tribute in the Delian League.
myus.e: The silting of the Maeander turned the gulf into a lake and marsh, and Pausanias says mosquitoes drove the people to move to Miletus, which absorbed the city by c. 200 BCE. Only a temple of Dionysus and scattered ruins remain.

military-frontier.t: Habsburg defensive belt along the Ottoman border, where soldier-settlers held land in return for military service and lived under army rule.
military-frontier.o: After Mohács the Habsburgs organised the Croatian and Slavonian border into fortified captaincies, formalised around 1553 with funds from the Austrian estates. Karlovac was founded in 1579 as a frontier fortress. Orthodox Vlach and Serb refugees from Ottoman lands were settled as Grenzer, receiving land and freedom from serfdom in return for service.
military-frontier.r: The frontier was run by army officers answering to the War Council in Vienna and Graz, not to the Croatian ban or Hungarian diet. Grenzer families lived in communal households, zadrugas, and owed lifelong military service. The 1630 Statuta Valachorum confirmed their privileges. In the 18th century the system was extended to Banat and Transylvania, guarding against plague as well as raids.
military-frontier.e: With the Ottoman threat gone, the frontier was dissolved between 1871 and 1881 and reattached to Croatia-Slavonia and Hungary. It left large Serb communities in Croatia, whose Krajina later became the base of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the 1990s.

marca-hispanica.t: The Carolingian frontier zone south and east of the Pyrenees, the cradle of the Catalan counties and of Catalonia itself.
marca-hispanica.o: After failing at Zaragoza in 778, Charlemagne's forces built a buffer zone against al-Andalus. Girona submitted in 785, and Louis the Pious, king of Aquitaine, took Barcelona in 801. The resulting counties, among them Barcelona, Girona, Urgell, Cerdanya, Osona, Empúries and Roussillon, became known as the Spanish March.
marca-hispanica.r: It was never a single state but a group of counties under counts appointed by the Frankish kings, sometimes grouped under one marquis such as Bernard of Septimania. The Gothic population kept the Visigothic law code. Revolts such as Aissó's in 826 and Muslim raids made it unstable. From 878 the counts, led by Wilfred the Hairy, made their offices hereditary.
marca-hispanica.e: Frankish authority faded through the 10th century. When the Caliphate's general Almanzor sacked Barcelona in 985 no help came, and in 988 Count Borrell II did not renew homage to the new Capetian king, a step later seen as the birth of Catalan independence.

march-of-verona.t: Imperial march in north-eastern Italy created by Otto I in 952, which joined Verona, Friuli and Istria to the German duchies until the Veronese cities rose against Barbarossa.
march-of-verona.o: In 952 Otto I forced Berengar II, King of Italy, to cede Verona, Friuli, Aquileia and Istria. Otto attached these lands to the Duchy of Bavaria under his brother Henry, creating a march that secured the Brenner and eastern Alpine routes between Germany and Italy. In 976 it passed with the new Duchy of Carinthia.
march-of-verona.r: The march was held by German dukes and margraves who rarely resided there, among them Henry I of Bavaria, dukes of Carinthia and Berthold of Zähringen; Hermann I, margrave of Verona in the 1060s, passed the title to his heirs, the margraves of Baden. Real power in the region shifted to bishops, the patriarchs of Aquileia and the growing city of Verona.
march-of-verona.e: In 1164 Verona, Vicenza, Padua and Treviso formed the Veronese League against Frederick Barbarossa, and the league later merged into the Lombard League. The march ceased to function, and Verona became a self-governing commune. The margraves of Baden kept the title.

mohu.t: Small ancient Estonian county between Ugandi and Järvamaa, known only from Henry of Livonia's chronicle.
mohu.o: Mõhu, called Mocha by Henry of Livonia, was a minor Estonian district in the east-central part of the country, between Ugandi, Vaiga and Järvamaa. It appears only briefly in the chronicle of the Livonian crusade in the early 13th century.
mohu.r: Like other Estonian lands, it was probably a union of a few parishes led by elders, with a hillfort for refuge. Nothing specific is recorded of its leaders or customs.
mohu.e: Mõhu was subdued with neighbouring districts during the conquest of Estonia, completed in 1224, and passed into the Bishopric of Dorpat.

march-of-ivrea.t: March in north-western Italy whose Anscarid rulers, Berengar II and Arduin, both seized the Italian crown.
march-of-ivrea.o: Around 888–891 Guy of Spoleto, contending for the Italian crown, created a march around Ivrea for his Burgundian ally Anscar, guarding the Alpine passes of the Aosta valley and the western Po plain. Anscar's descendants, the Anscarids, held it for more than a century.
march-of-ivrea.r: The margraves of Ivrea controlled a large area of Piedmont and Lombardy. Anscar's grandson Berengar II, after exile in Germany, made himself King of Italy in 950 with his son Adalbert, until Otto I forced him to submit in 952 and deposed him in 961. A later margrave, Arduin, was elected king in 1002 in opposition to the German emperor Henry II.
march-of-ivrea.e: Henry II defeated Arduin, who retired to the monastery of Fruttuaria and died in 1015. The march was then broken up, its lands divided among bishops and other families, notably the Arduinici of Turin.

mandubii.t: Small Gallic people of Burgundy whose hilltop town Alesia was the scene of Vercingetorix's last stand against Caesar in 52 BCE.
mandubii.o: The Mandubii lived in the Auxois district of northern Burgundy, between the Aedui, Lingones and Sequani, and were probably clients of the Aedui. Their oppidum Alesia stood on Mont Auxois, above modern Alise-Sainte-Reine.
mandubii.r: Almost nothing is known of their society before the siege that made their town famous.
mandubii.e: In 52 BCE Vercingetorix took refuge in Alesia, and Caesar surrounded it with double lines of siege works. To save food, the defenders expelled the Mandubii with their wives and children, but Caesar would not let them pass, and they were left to starve between the lines. After the surrender Alesia lived on as a Gallo-Roman town.

messapians.t: Iapygian people of the Salento peninsula in Apulia, long-time rivals of Greek Taras, with their own language, fortified towns and kings.
messapians.o: The Messapians emerged in the heel of Italy in the early 1st millennium BCE as one of three Iapygian peoples, with the Daunians and Peucetians. Ancient writers traced them to Illyria or Crete; modern scholars note links across the Adriatic but see a largely local formation. Their main centres included Uria (Oria), Rudiae, Manduria, Cavallino and Egnatia.
messapians.r: Messapian towns had massive stone walls, chamber tombs and painted trozzella vases. They wrote Messapic, an Indo-European language, in an alphabet borrowed from the Greeks of Taras, and their many inscriptions are a key source. Kings are mentioned occasionally, like Artas, who supplied javelin-men to Athens in 413 BCE. They inflicted a heavy defeat on Taras and Rhegion around 473 BCE, and at Manduria in 338 BCE they killed the Spartan king Archidamus III.
messapians.e: Rome defeated the Messapians and their Sallentini neighbours in 267–266 BCE, and their towns became allies and later municipia. Messapic was still written into the 1st century BCE before giving way to Latin. The poet Ennius, born at Rudiae, was of Messapian background.

megiddo.t: Megiddo, a fortified Canaanite city guarding a key pass into the Jezreel Valley, scene of Thutmose III's famous victory and origin of the name Armageddon.
megiddo.o: Megiddo had been a walled town since the Early Bronze Age. Its Middle Bronze Age kingdom, rebuilt with massive ramparts and a palace in the early 2nd millennium BCE, controlled the route through the Carmel ridge along which armies and caravans travelled between Egypt and Syria.
megiddo.r: Kings ruled from a palace near the city gate, alongside a temple to Canaanite gods. In c. 1457 BCE Thutmose III of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom defeated a coalition led by the king of Kadesh outside the city and besieged it for seven months. Afterwards Megiddo was an Egyptian vassal; its ruler Biridiya wrote several Amarna letters.
megiddo.e: The Canaanite city was destroyed in the 12th century BCE as Egyptian power in Canaan collapsed. A later town became part of the Kingdom of Israel, and the hoard of carved Megiddo ivories survives from its last Canaanite palace.

margraviate-of-austria.t: The Babenberg march on the Danube, first named Ostarrîchi in 996, from which the Duchy of Austria and the Habsburg state grew.
margraviate-of-austria.o: After Otto I's victory over the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955, a march was established on the Danube east of Bavaria. In 976 Otto II gave it to Leopold of Babenberg. A document of Otto III in 996 names the area 'Ostarrîchi', the earliest form of the name Austria.
margraviate-of-austria.r: The Babenberg margraves pushed the frontier east to the March and the Leitha, encouraging settlement and founding monasteries. Their seat moved from Melk to Tulln, Klosterneuburg and finally Vienna around 1145. Leopold III, founder of Klosterneuburg and Heiligenkreuz, was later canonised and became Austria's patron saint.
margraviate-of-austria.e: In 1156 Frederick Barbarossa raised the margraviate to the Duchy of Austria by the Privilegium Minus, compensating Henry II Jasomirgott for giving up Bavaria. The new duchy, with special rights of inheritance, formed the nucleus of Habsburg power.

marwanid-badajoz.t: The autonomous muwallad lordship founded by the rebel Ibn Marwan, who built the city of Badajoz and defied the emirs of Córdoba.
marwanid-badajoz.o: Abd al-Rahman ibn Marwan, known as al-Jilliqi, 'the Galician', was a muwallad leader from Mérida who rebelled against the Emirate of Córdoba. After a period of revolt and an alliance with Alfonso III of Asturias, the emir Muhammad I allowed him in about 875 to settle at Badajoz, which he fortified as his capital.
marwanid-badajoz.r: Ibn Marwan and his descendants ruled the lower Guadiana as virtually independent lords, drawing support from muwallads and Christians and shifting between Córdoba and the Christian north. Their lordship was one of several autonomous states that split al-Andalus during the fitna of the late 9th century.
marwanid-badajoz.e: As Abd al-Rahman III restored central authority, he took Badajoz in 929 or 930 and ended the Marwanid lordship. Badajoz remained an important city and later became the capital of the Taifa of Badajoz.

margraviate-of-lower-lusatia.t: The march of Lusatia between the Elbe and the Oder, a homeland of the Sorbs passed between Germany, Poland and Bohemia before Prussia took it in 1815.
margraviate-of-lower-lusatia.o: After Gero died in 965, Otto I made the Saxon Eastern March, later called the March of Lusatia, a separate margraviate. In 1002 the Polish ruler Bolesław I seized it, and Poland held it until 1031. From 1136 it was held mainly by the Wettin margraves of Meissen.
margraviate-of-lower-lusatia.r: The land around Lübben, Cottbus and Guben was largely rural, with a strong Sorbian-speaking population. Lordship changed often: Brandenburg held it from 1304, and in 1367 Emperor Charles IV bought it for the Bohemian crown. The estates of the land kept substantial self-government under these distant rulers.
margraviate-of-lower-lusatia.e: The Peace of Prague of 1635 transferred Lower Lusatia from Bohemia to the Electorate of Saxony. After Saxony sided with Napoleon, the Congress of Vienna gave it to Prussia in 1815, and it became part of the province of Brandenburg. The Lower Sorbian language is still spoken around Cottbus.

moesi.t: Thracian people of the Danube plain who gave their name to the Roman province of Moesia.
moesi.o: Known mainly from Roman sources, the Moesi lived along the right bank of the Danube in modern Serbia and northern Bulgaria, probably related to the Mysians of Asia Minor. They appear as a distinct people from the late centuries BCE.
moesi.r: Little is recorded of their institutions. They lived in tribal communities of farmers and herders in the valleys south of the Danube, neighbours of the Triballi and the Scordisci, and resisted Roman advances from Macedonia.
moesi.e: Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated them in his campaign of 29 BCE, and their land was organised as the province of Moesia early in the 1st century CE. The province became a key Danube frontier with legionary bases at Singidunum, Viminacium and Novae.

megalopolis.t: 'Great City' of Arcadia, founded as a bulwark against Sparta, home of the statesman Philopoemen and the historian Polybius.
megalopolis.o: Megalopolis was founded between 371 and 368 BCE as the capital of the new Arcadian League, by moving the people of around forty villages of south-western Arcadia into a single city on the Helisson river. Its purpose was to block Spartan routes north and to give the Arcadians a shared centre.
megalopolis.r: The city was laid out on a grand scale with walls of more than 8 kilometres, the largest theatre in Greece and the Thersilion, a hall for the federal assembly. Its population never filled the walls. Megalopolis was consistently hostile to Sparta and pro-Macedonian. Its tyrant Lydiadas voluntarily laid down power and took it into the Achaean League in 235 BCE.
megalopolis.e: Cleomenes III of Sparta sacked it in 223 BCE, but it was rebuilt and produced the Achaean leader Philopoemen and the historian Polybius. It lost independence after the Achaean War of 146 BCE and declined under Roman rule; Strabo called it a great desert.

march-of-montferrat.t: Marquisate in Piedmont whose Aleramici and Palaiologos rulers were crusaders and kings in the East, raised to a duchy in 1574.
march-of-montferrat.o: In 967 Otto I confirmed Aleramo, a nobleman of Frankish descent, as margrave of lands in the hills south of the Po between Turin and Genoa, later called Montferrat. His descendants, the Aleramici, ruled it for more than three centuries.
march-of-montferrat.r: The Aleramici were famed crusaders: Conrad of Montferrat defended Tyre and was elected King of Jerusalem in 1192, and Boniface I led the Fourth Crusade and became King of Thessalonica. In 1306 the march passed to Theodore I Palaiologos, son of the Byzantine emperor Andronikos II, whose family ruled until 1533. Casale Monferrato became the capital in the 15th century. The territory produced grain and wine.
march-of-montferrat.e: After the last Palaiologos died in 1533, Charles V awarded Montferrat to Federico II Gonzaga of Mantua in 1536. In 1574 Emperor Maximilian II raised it to a duchy. The Gonzaga held it until 1708, when it passed to Savoy.

menapii.t: Belgic people of the Scheldt and lower Rhine who held off Caesar for years by retreating into their marshes and forests.
menapii.o: The Menapii lived in the low, marshy lands of Flanders and the southern Netherlands, from the Scheldt to the Rhine. They joined the Belgic league in 57 BCE.
menapii.r: They lived in scattered farmsteads and avoided pitched battle, withdrawing into woods and swamps. In 55 BCE the Germanic Usipetes and Tencteri crossed the Rhine and seized part of their land.
menapii.e: Caesar campaigned against them in 56 and 55 BCE and finally subdued them in 53 BCE by burning their settlements. Under Rome their capital was Castellum Menapiorum (Cassel). The usurper Carausius, who ruled Britain from 286 CE, was a Menapian.

mastieni.t: An Iberian people of the Cartagena region, whose town Mastia marked the limit set on Roman shipping in a 4th-century BCE treaty with Carthage.
mastieni.o: The Mastieni lived in south-eastern Iberia, around modern Cartagena and Murcia. Greek writers knew them from the 6th century BCE, and they belonged to the Iberian culture of the Mediterranean coast.
mastieni.r: Almost nothing is known of their institutions. Their chief town, Mastia, is named in the second treaty between Rome and Carthage, of 348 BCE, as the point beyond which Romans could not trade or found cities. The region was rich in silver and lead, later intensively mined.
mastieni.e: Around 227 BCE the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal founded Qart Hadasht, later Carthago Nova, probably on or near the site of Mastia, making it the capital of Barcid Iberia. The Mastieni name then disappears.

moravian-serbia.t: Prince Lazar's Serbian state on the Morava, which led the resistance to the Ottomans at Kosovo in 1389 and founded a rich school of church art.
moravian-serbia.o: After the Serbian Empire broke up, Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović, a court official under Dušan, built the strongest of the successor states in the Morava valley. With Tvrtko I he destroyed Nikola Altomanović in 1373, and by 1379 he was the leading Serbian ruler, with Kruševac as his capital.
moravian-serbia.r: Lazar ruled with nobles bound by family ties, including his son-in-law Vuk Branković. The silver mines of Novo Brdo and Rudnik paid for the state, and Lazar reconciled the Serbian church with Constantinople in 1375. Churches such as Ravanica and Lazarica gave their name to the Morava school of architecture.
moravian-serbia.e: Lazar died at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. His widow Milica and son Stefan Lazarević became Ottoman vassals. After fighting at Ankara in 1402, Stefan received the title of despot from Byzantium, and the state became the Serbian Despotate.

moche.t: A coastal civilisation of northern Peru that built huge adobe pyramids and produced the most lifelike portrait pottery and metalwork of the ancient Andes.
moche.o: The Moche, or Mochica, culture developed around 100 CE in the river valleys of Peru's north coast, especially the Moche and Chicama valleys near modern Trujillo. Local elites drew on earlier coastal traditions such as Cupisnique and Salinar and extended irrigation canals across the desert.
moche.r: Moche society was ruled by warrior-priest lords. Its capital at Huacas de Moche had the Huaca del Sol, one of the largest adobe structures in the Americas, and the painted Huaca de la Luna. The tombs of the Lord of Sipán, found in 1987, and the Lady of Cao show the wealth of gold, silver and copper regalia. Moche pottery includes realistic portrait vessels and painted scenes of warfare, sacrifice and daily life.
moche.e: Heavy El Niño floods and droughts in the 6th century disrupted Moche society, and its centres shifted north to Pampa Grande and Galindo before collapsing around 800 CE. Its traditions passed to the Sicán and the Kingdom of Chimor.

metapontum.t: Achaean Greek city on the Gulf of Taranto, rich in grain, where Pythagoras spent his last years.
metapontum.o: Achaean settlers founded Metapontum in the 7th century BCE on the coastal plain between the Bradano and Basento rivers. Ancient sources say Sybaris encouraged the colony to block the expansion of Spartan Taras. Earlier native and Greek settlement existed nearby, and the city grew quickly on the plain.
metapontum.r: Metapontum's wealth came from grain, celebrated on its coins with an ear of barley and by a 'golden harvest' it dedicated at Delphi. Archaeologists have traced the division of its countryside into regular plots and many farmhouses. The Tavole Palatine, fifteen standing columns of a temple of Hera, survive outside the town. Pythagoras moved there after being driven from Croton, and his school stayed influential in the city.
metapontum.e: Metapontum joined the Athenian side in 413 BCE and later suffered from Lucanian pressure. It came under Roman control after the war with Pyrrhus around 272 BCE, sided with Hannibal and was abandoned by many of its people when he left Italy in 207 BCE. It survived as a small Roman town.

march-of-turin.t: March of the Arduinici in Piedmont whose heiress Adelaide of Susa brought its lands to the house of Savoy.
march-of-turin.o: Around 941 King Hugh of Arles or his successor reorganised the western Alps and Piedmont, giving Arduin Glaber control of Turin and the Susa valley. Arduin drove out Arab raiders based at Fraxinetum from the passes, and his family, the Arduinici, held the march for 150 years.
march-of-turin.r: The margraves controlled the routes over the Mont Cenis and Mont Genèvre passes, a source of wealth and strategic weight. Ulric Manfred II (died 1034) extended the march and founded monasteries. His daughter Adelaide of Susa ruled for over half a century, married Otto of Savoy, and was one of the most powerful figures in northern Italy, the mother-in-law of Emperor Henry IV.
march-of-turin.e: When Adelaide died in 1091, the march broke up among her heirs, local lords and the growing commune of Turin. Her Savoyard descendants eventually inherited Turin and Piedmont, the foundation of the later Savoy state.

massagetae.t: A powerful nomadic confederation east of the Caspian, best known for Queen Tomyris, whose warriors defeated and killed Cyrus the Great in 530 BCE.
massagetae.o: Greek historians, above all Herodotus, describe the Massagetae living beyond the Araxes, usually identified with the Amu Darya or Syr Darya, on the plains east of the Caspian Sea from the 6th century BCE. They were related to the Saka and are often treated as one of the major Saka groupings.
massagetae.r: Herodotus describes a people fighting both on horseback and on foot with bows, lances and bronze-headed battle-axes, using gold and bronze but no iron or silver. They worshipped the sun, to which they sacrificed horses, and lived on herds and fish. Some groups occupied the deltas of the Amu Darya, near the farming towns of the Kingdom of Khwarazm.
massagetae.e: After their victory over Cyrus, the Massagetae fade from detailed record. They are mentioned in Alexander the Great's campaigns in Sogdiana, then dissolve into later steppe groupings such as the Dahae and the peoples displaced by the Yuezhi. Their name was later revived by Byzantine writers as a learned label for Huns.

muisca-confederation.t: A union of chiefdoms in Colombia's eastern highlands whose gold offerings in Lake Guatavita gave rise to the legend of El Dorado.
muisca-confederation.o: The Muisca settled the high plateau of Cundinamarca and Boyacá, in the Eastern Ranges of the Colombian Andes, and by around 800 their chiefdoms had taken shape. Over the following centuries they grouped into larger confederations led by the zipa in the south and the zaque in the north.
muisca-confederation.r: Muisca society was divided between the Zipazgo of Bacatá in the south, the Zacazgo of Hunza in the north, and independent territories such as Iraca and Tundama. Rulers inherited power through the maternal line, from uncle to nephew. The Muisca traded salt from Zipaquirá and Nemocón, emeralds and cotton cloth for gold, which they cast into tunjos, votive figures. The installation of a new ruler at Lake Guatavita, covered in gold dust, became the legend of El Dorado.
muisca-confederation.e: Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada led a Spanish expedition into Muisca lands in 1537, defeating the zipa and zaque within two years. Santa Fe de Bogotá was founded in 1538 as the centre of the New Kingdom of Granada. The Muisca language died out in the 18th century.

miguelist-portugal.t: The absolutist regime of King Miguel I, whose seizure of the throne in 1828 sparked Portugal's Liberal Wars.
miguelist-portugal.o: On John VI's death in 1826 his heir Pedro, emperor of Brazil, granted Portugal a constitutional Charter and abdicated for his daughter Maria II, naming his brother Miguel regent. In 1828 Miguel, backed by absolutists and the Church, had the Cortes proclaim him king.
miguelist-portugal.r: Miguel abolished the Charter and ruled as an absolute monarch, persecuting liberals, many of whom fled abroad or to the Azores. He enjoyed popular support in the countryside and among the clergy, but most European powers refused to recognise him. The liberals held Terceira and formed a government in exile.
miguelist-portugal.e: Pedro returned from Brazil, landed near Porto in 1832 and endured a long siege before liberal forces took Lisbon in 1833. Miguel surrendered by the Concession of Evoramonte in May 1834 and went into permanent exile, and Maria II was restored to the Kingdom of Portugal.

marcomanni.t: A Suebian Germanic people who settled Bohemia and fought Rome in the Marcomannic Wars, the hardest frontier struggle of Marcus Aurelius' reign.
marcomanni.o: The Marcomanni ('border men') first appear among Ariovistus' followers in 58 BCE, probably living near the upper Rhine and Main. Around 9 BCE, under pressure from Roman campaigns led by Drusus, their leader Maroboduus led them east into Bohemia, the former land of the Boii, where they formed the core of a powerful kingdom.
marcomanni.r: After Maroboduus fell, the Marcomanni were usually ruled by kings who acted as Roman clients, receiving subsidies and trading through Carnuntum on the Danube. Roman goods are common in their graves. In 166 they and the Quadi broke through the frontier, besieging Aquileia in Italy and sparking the Marcomannic Wars, which Marcus Aurelius fought until his death in 180.
marcomanni.e: Commodus made peace in 180, and the Marcomanni remained a frontier people for two more centuries, with a queen, Fritigil, converting to Christianity around 396. They faded from the record in the 5th century, many joining the Huns or merging into the people later called Bavarians.

mengujekids.t: A Turkish dynasty of the upper Euphrates whose masterpiece, the Great Mosque and Hospital of Divrigi, is a World Heritage Site.
mengujekids.o: After the battle of Manzikert in 1071, the Turkmen commander Mengujek Gazi took Erzincan, Kemah, Divrigi and Sebinkarahisar on the upper Euphrates, establishing a small principality between the Danishmendids, the Saltukids and the Byzantine and Georgian frontiers.
mengujekids.r: The Mengujekids were patrons of Persian culture and architecture. Fakhr al-Din Bahramshah of Erzincan, who ruled for some sixty years, received the dedication of Nizami's poem Makhzan al-Asrar. In 1228-1229 Ahmad Shah of Divrigi and his wife Turan Malik built the Great Mosque and Hospital of Divrigi, whose carved stone portals are among the most extraordinary in medieval Islamic art. Their towns had large Armenian and Greek populations.
mengujekids.e: The Sultanate of Rum absorbed the Erzincan branch around 1228 under Kayqubad I. The Divrigi branch survived as Seljuk and then Mongol vassals until it disappears from the record in 1277.

margraviate-of-upper-lusatia.t: The land of Bautzen and Görlitz, a Sorb homeland ruled for centuries by Bohemia, famed for its Six Towns League and Herrnhut.
margraviate-of-upper-lusatia.o: The area around Bautzen, the land of the Slavic Milceni, belonged to the Margraviate of Meissen. In 1158 Frederick Barbarossa granted the land of Bautzen to Vladislaus II of Bohemia, starting a long Bohemian connection. From the 15th century the region came to be called Upper Lusatia, in contrast to Lower Lusatia.
margraviate-of-upper-lusatia.r: Upper Lusatia was ruled by distant Bohemian kings but largely governed by its estates and towns. In 1346 Bautzen, Görlitz, Zittau, Lauban, Kamenz and Löbau formed the Six Towns League, protecting trade routes. The mystic Jakob Böhme lived in Görlitz, and in 1722 Moravian refugees founded Herrnhut under Count Zinzendorf.
margraviate-of-upper-lusatia.e: The Peace of Prague of 1635 transferred Upper Lusatia to the Electorate of Saxony. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave the north-eastern half, including Görlitz, to Prussia. Today it is split between Saxony and Poland, with a Sorbian minority around Bautzen.

maroneia.t: Chian colony on the coast of Thrace, famed since Homer for its strong wine.
maroneia.o: Maroneia was founded by settlers from Chios c. 650 BCE on the Thracian coast east of Abdera, near the land of the Cicones. Its name recalled Maron, the priest of Apollo who gave Odysseus the potent wine he used to intoxicate the Cyclops.
maroneia.r: Maroneia's wealth came from wine and trade with Thracians, and its coins showed a prancing horse and vines. It paid tribute in the Delian League and later joined the Second Athenian League. The city's Dionysus sanctuary and theatre reflected its wine economy, and it built a strong harbour.
maroneia.e: Maroneia passed under Philip II, then the Ptolemaic Empire and the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia. Philip V's troops massacred many citizens in 184 BCE. Rome made it a free city, and it came under Roman control by 146 BCE.

margraviate-of-burgau.t: Swabian margraviate between Ulm and Augsburg that the Habsburgs held for five centuries as part of Further Austria, ruled from Günzburg.
margraviate-of-burgau.o: The margraves of Burgau, a branch of the counts of Berg, held lands on the Danube and the lower Mindel and Günz rivers from the early 13th century, using the margravial title from about 1212. When their line died out in 1301, the margraviate passed to the Habsburgs, who added it to their scattered Swabian possessions.
margraviate-of-burgau.r: Burgau was a weak territory: the Habsburgs often pledged it, and many monasteries, imperial cities and nobles inside its borders claimed their own rights, leaving the margrave chiefly with high justice and taxation. From 1609 Günzburg was the residence of Margrave Charles of Burgau, son of Archduke Ferdinand II and Philippine Welser. In the 18th century Günzburg housed an important Austrian mint.
margraviate-of-burgau.e: After Austria's defeat by Napoleon, the Peace of Pressburg of 1805 transferred Burgau to the Electorate of Bavaria, soon the Kingdom of Bavaria. Its lands now lie in the Bavarian district of Swabia.

mari.t: Mari, a city-kingdom on the middle Euphrates whose royal archives give the most detailed picture of diplomacy and daily politics in the age of Hammurabi.
mari.o: Mari was founded c. 2900 BCE at Tell Hariri as a planned circular city controlling river traffic between Syria and southern Mesopotamia. Rebuilt after a destruction, it flourished c. 2500 to 2300 BCE as a rival of Ebla, then was governed by military governors, the shakkanakku, under the Akkadian Empire and its successors.
mari.r: Around 1800 BCE the Amorite Lim dynasty ruled from a vast palace of some 260 rooms. Mari lived from river tolls, trade in tin and textiles, and irrigated farming, while its kings negotiated constantly with tribal groups. The archive of over 20,000 tablets, written in Akkadian, records letters, prophecies, treaties and court life under Zimri-Lim.
mari.e: Shamshi-Adad's Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia briefly absorbed Mari before Zimri-Lim regained the throne. His former ally Hammurabi of the Babylonian Empire conquered the city and destroyed it in the late 1760s BCE. It never recovered as a capital, but French excavations from 1933 made its palace and archive famous.

mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate.t: A failed division of Mount Lebanon into Christian and Druze districts, which ended in the civil war of 1860.
mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate.o: After the end of the Mount Lebanon Emirate in 1842 and fighting between Druze and Maronites, the Ottomans and the European powers agreed to divide the mountain along the Beirut-Damascus road. A Maronite qaimaqam governed the north and a Druze qaimaqam the south, both under the Ottoman governor in Beirut.
mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate.r: The division ignored the many mixed villages, and the 1845 rules of Shakib Efendi added councils representing each community, which did not end the tensions. In 1858 Maronite peasants of Kisrawan led by Tanyus Shahin rose against their Khazin overlords and expelled them, a social revolt that alarmed Druze lords in the south.
mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate.e: In 1860 a civil war broke out in which Druze fighters killed thousands of Christians, followed by a massacre in Damascus. France sent troops, and an international commission created the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate in 1861.

mira.t: Mira, the strongest of the vassal kingdoms carved out of Arzawa, whose king's name was read on the Karabel rock relief near Izmir.
mira.o: After Mursili II of the Hittite Empire defeated Arzawa c. 1320 BCE, he made Mashuiluwa, a prince who had sought refuge at the Hittite court, king of Mira, the land around the upper Maeander valley and its neighbour Kuwaliya.
mira.r: Mira's kings ruled by treaty with the Hittite great king, and their line included Kupanta-Kurunta. A reading of the Karabel relief near Izmir, published in 1998, names Tarkasnawa, king of Mira, showing his realm reached towards the Aegean. Its people spoke Luwian.
mira.e: Mashuiluwa rebelled and was deposed, but Mira stayed a Hittite vassal until the empire collapsed c. 1180 BCE. The western Anatolian kingdoms then disappear from records; the region later became part of the Kingdom of Lydia.

medulli.t: Alpine people of the Maurienne valley, among the mountain peoples finally subdued by Augustus.
medulli.o: Strabo places the Medulli on the highest mountains above the confluence of the Isère and the Rhône, and they are generally located in the Maurienne, the valley of the Arc in Savoy. They controlled routes towards the passes into Italy.
medulli.r: Almost nothing is known of their society beyond their mountain economy of herding and pass trade. They appear among the communities of the Cottian Alps.
medulli.e: Their name is listed among the Alpine peoples conquered by Augustus on the Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie, erected in 7 to 6 BCE. Their land was divided between the Cottian Alps and neighbouring districts.

manapii.t: People of south-east Ireland named by Ptolemy, with a town called Manapia, sharing their name with the Menapii of the Low Countries.
manapii.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Manapii on the east coast of Ireland, south of the Cauci, usually located around Wicklow or north Wexford, with a settlement named Manapia. Their name matches the Menapii of Belgic Gaul, which has led to suggestions of migration or trading links across the sea.
manapii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Some scholars connect them with later Irish population names such as the Monaig, recorded in Leinster and Ulster, and with the Fir Manach who gave their name to Fermanagh, but these links rest only on the similarity of names.
manapii.e: The Manapii do not appear in later records. Their part of the coast later lay within the Kingdom of Leinster, and especially the lands of the Ui Chennselaig.

mesembria.t: Dorian Greek city on a rocky peninsula of the Bulgarian Black Sea coast, whose long life as a trading port survives in the old town of Nesebar.
mesembria.o: Mesembria took its name from an earlier Thracian settlement called Menebria. Greek colonists from Megara and its colonies Chalcedon and Byzantium settled there around the end of the 6th century BCE; Herodotus says refugees from Byzantium and Chalcedon came after the Persian suppression of the Ionian Revolt. The narrow isthmus made it easy to defend.
mesembria.r: A Doric-speaking polis with council and assembly, Mesembria lived from sea trade, fishing and exchange with the Thracians of the interior, and struck coins in silver and later gold. It competed with its northern neighbour Apollonia and sometimes fought it. Hellenistic Mesembria built strong walls and temples to Apollo and Zeus.
mesembria.e: Roman forces under Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus subdued the West Pontic cities in 72-71 BCE. Mesembria became part of the province of Thrace and later an important Byzantine fortress and bishopric, contested with the Bulgarians. Its Byzantine churches and ancient walls make Nesebar a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

mount-lebanon-emirate.t: The autonomous emirate of the Druze and Maronite mountain, ruled by the Ma'n and Shihab families and the forerunner of modern Lebanon.
mount-lebanon-emirate.o: After the Ottoman conquest of 1516, the Druze chiefs of the Shuf mountains were left to govern themselves as tax farmers. The Ma'n family rose to dominate them, and under Fakhr al-Din II (1591-1633) their emirate extended over much of Lebanon, Galilee and the coast.
mount-lebanon-emirate.r: The emirs ruled a feudal society of Druze and Maronite lords and peasants from Deir al-Qamar. Fakhr al-Din II allied with Tuscany, lived in exile in Italy in 1613-1618 and promoted silk production, but was executed by the Ottomans in 1635. In 1697 the Shihab family succeeded the Ma'ns. Bashir II (1789-1840), who became Christian, built the palace of Beiteddine and sided with Muhammad Ali of Egypt.
mount-lebanon-emirate.e: When the Ottomans and Britain expelled the Egyptians in 1840, Bashir II went into exile. His successor Bashir III was deposed in 1842 amid Druze-Maronite fighting, and the Ottomans replaced the emirate with the Mount Lebanon Double Qaimaqamate.

melingoi.t: Slavic tribe of the Taygetus mountains in the Peloponnese that kept a semi-independent life under Byzantine and Frankish rule for centuries.
melingoi.o: The Melingoi were descendants of Slavs who settled in the Peloponnese in the late 6th and 7th centuries. By the 9th century they lived on the slopes of Mount Taygetus, west of Sparta. Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio describes their revolt and subjugation by the general Theoktistos Bryennios in the 840s.
melingoi.r: Living in mountain villages under their own leaders, the Melingoi paid the Byzantine state a small fixed tribute, 60 gold coins a year according to Constantine VII, rather than ordinary taxes. They revolted again in the 920s and had their tribute raised before it was reduced once more. The Chronicle of the Morea shows them still distinct in the 13th century.
melingoi.e: After the Frankish conquest, William of Villehardouin built Mistras and other castles in 1249 partly to control them; they later served as soldiers for both Franks and Byzantines. Gradually Christianised and Hellenised, they disappear as a separate group by the late Middle Ages.
melingoi.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

methone-pieria.t: Eretrian colony on the Macedonian coast whose siege in 354 BCE cost Philip II an eye, and whose pottery bears some of the oldest Greek writing.
methone-pieria.o: Methone was founded on the coast of Pieria, on the Thermaic Gulf, by settlers from Eretria c. 733 BCE; Plutarch says they were Eretrians driven out of Corcyra. The site, on a low hill by the sea, had been inhabited since the Neolithic.
methone-pieria.r: Methone was a trading port linking the Aegean with Macedonian timber and metals. Excavations since 2003 have found a deposit of pottery from c. 700 BCE inscribed with some of the earliest Greek alphabetic writing, as well as metalworking debris. In the Classical period it was an ally of Athens and a base for Athenian interference in Macedon.
methone-pieria.e: Philip II of the Kingdom of Macedon besieged Methone in 354 BCE, losing an eye to an arrow. After its surrender he razed the city and divided its land among Macedonians. The site later became a small village.

march-of-friuli.t: Carolingian frontier march in north-eastern Italy whose margrave Berengar became King of Italy and emperor.
march-of-friuli.o: After Duke Hrodgaud's revolt in 776, Charlemagne replaced the Lombard dukes of Friuli with Frankish officials. The territory was expanded into a march facing the Avars and the Slavs, and its margraves commanded forces that, under Eric of Friuli, captured the Avar Ring and its treasure in 796.
march-of-friuli.r: The march was a military command reaching from the Alps to Istria and into Pannonia, with Cividale as its centre. After 828 it was reorganised, and from about 846 it was held by the Unruoching family, beginning with Eberhard, a cultured noble who married Louis the Pious's daughter Gisela and owned a notable library. His son Berengar became margrave in 874.
march-of-friuli.e: Berengar of Friuli was elected King of Italy in 888 and crowned emperor in 915, while Hungarian raids devastated the region. In 952 Otto I took Friuli from Italian control and attached it, with Verona, to the Duchy of Bavaria as the March of Verona.

meldi.t: Small Gallic people of the Marne valley whose town Iatinum became Meaux.
meldi.o: The Meldi lived on the Marne east of the Parisii. Caesar mentions that in 54 BCE some of the ships for his second expedition to Britain were built in their territory.
meldi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions.
meldi.e: Under Rome they formed a small civitas with Iatinum as its chief town, later called Meldi after the people, the origin of Meaux, which became a bishopric.

motya.t: Phoenician island city in the Stagnone lagoon of western Sicily, a major Punic trading base until Dionysius I of Syracuse destroyed it in 397 BCE.
motya.o: Motya was founded by Phoenicians in the late 8th century BCE on the small island of San Pantaleo, off the western tip of Sicily. Like other Phoenician sites, it chose an offshore island with sheltered anchorage close to a native hinterland, here the Elymian towns of Segesta and Eryx. It soon came within Carthage's sphere.
motya.r: Motya was a busy port and craft centre, with dye works, potteries and a small artificial basin. A causeway linked it to the mainland, and walls with towers enclosed the island in the 6th century BCE. Its tophet, a sacred precinct for child burials, and its temples show Phoenician religion; the marble Motya Charioteer, a Greek masterpiece of about 470 BCE, was found there in 1979.
motya.e: In 397 BCE Dionysius I of Syracuse besieged Motya, building a mole across the lagoon and using siege towers and catapults; the city fell after fierce street fighting. Carthage did not rebuild it and moved the survivors to Lilybaeum on the mainland. The island was bought by Joseph Whitaker, who began its excavation in the early 20th century.

messene.t: City founded by Epaminondas in 369 BCE to free the Messenians from centuries of Spartan helotry, with some of the finest surviving Greek fortifications.
messene.o: For centuries the Messenians had been helots, forced to work their land for Sparta. After defeating Sparta at Leuctra, the Theban general Epaminondas invaded the Peloponnese and in 369 BCE founded Messene on the slopes of Mount Ithome, calling back Messenians scattered across the Greek world. Sparta refused for decades to recognise the new state.
messene.r: Messene was built from scratch with a ring of stone walls some 9 kilometres long, towers and the great Arcadian Gate. It had a council and assembly and celebrated its restored identity in cults of Zeus Ithomatas and the hero Aristomenes. Fearing Sparta, it sought protection from Thebes, then Philip II and later the Hellenistic kings.
messene.e: Messene joined the Achaean League in 191 BCE, revolted, and in 182 BCE executed the captured Achaean general Philopoemen before being forced back. After the Achaean War in 146 BCE it passed under Roman rule. Excavations have uncovered its theatre, stadium and agora, among the best-preserved in Greece.

margraviate-of-brandenburg.t: The electorate of the Hohenzollerns around Berlin, a sandy frontier march that grew into the Kingdom of Prussia.
margraviate-of-brandenburg.o: Albert the Bear secured Brandenburg an der Havel in 1157, after inheriting it from the Hevelli prince Pribislav-Henry, and called himself Margrave of Brandenburg. His Ascanian successors pushed east to the Oder, encouraging German settlement and founding towns, including the twin towns of Berlin and Cölln in the 13th century.
margraviate-of-brandenburg.r: The Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed the margrave as an elector. In 1415 Emperor Sigismund gave Brandenburg to the Hohenzollern Frederick VI of Nuremberg. Joachim II introduced Lutheranism in 1539. The Great Elector, Frederick William, rebuilt after the Thirty Years' War, welcoming Huguenot refugees in 1685 and creating a standing army.
margraviate-of-brandenburg.e: In 1701 Elector Frederick III crowned himself King in Prussia, and Brandenburg became the heartland of the Prussian state. The margraviate ended formally with the Empire in 1806; it later became a Prussian province and is today the German state of Brandenburg around Berlin.
margraviate-of-brandenburg.re: Catholic Christianity, then Lutheranism and Calvinism

melid.t: Melid, a Neo-Hittite kingdom at Malatya on the upper Euphrates, ruled by heirs of the Hittite royal house until Assyria annexed it.
melid.o: Melid, at Arslantepe near Malatya, had been an important town since the 4th millennium BCE. After the Hittite Empire fell c. 1180 BCE, a dynasty descended from Kuzi-Teshub of the Kingdom of Carchemish ruled the region, also called Kammanu, as an independent kingdom.
melid.r: Its kings wrote Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions and adorned the gate of their citadel with reliefs of lions and of the king pouring offerings to the storm god, now in Ankara. Melid lived from the farmland of the Malatya plain and the river crossing, paying tribute to the Assyrian Empire or the Kingdom of Urartu.
melid.e: Sargon II of the Assyrian Empire deposed King Tarhunazi in 712 BCE, made Melid an Assyrian province and gave part of it to Kummuh. The Neo-Hittite citadel at Arslantepe was later abandoned.

mycenaean-kingdom-of-iolkos.t: Mycenaean palace centre on the Gulf of Pagasae in Thessaly, the legendary home of Jason and the Argonauts.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-iolkos.o: Iolkos lies at modern Volos, on the Pagasetic Gulf, the best harbour of Thessaly. Settlement there goes back to the Early Bronze Age, and by c. 1600 BCE a Mycenaean elite had appeared. Excavations at Kastro and especially Dimini, where a 14th to 13th century BCE palatial complex was uncovered, suggest a palace centre in the area.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-iolkos.r: Little is known of its government. The Dimini complex had large buildings with storerooms and workshops, and Linear B inscribed stirrup jars hint at contact with other palace centres. Tholos tombs at Kapakli and Dimini show a wealthy elite. Greek myth made Iolkos the city of Pelias and the starting point of Jason's voyage on the Argo.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-iolkos.e: The Dimini complex was abandoned c. 1200 BCE, during the general collapse of palace societies, though Iolkos itself stayed inhabited. In 293 BCE Demetrius Poliorcetes moved its population into his new city of Demetrias nearby.

maeatae.t: Confederation just north of the Antonine Wall whose raids drew Septimius Severus to Scotland, and whose name survives in Dumyat near Stirling.
maeatae.o: The Maeatae are first named by Cassius Dio, who describes them as living close to the wall that divided the island, with the Caledonians beyond them. They seem to have been a grouping of peoples in the Forth valley and Stirling area that emerged in the later 2nd century, perhaps including the earlier Venicones.
maeatae.r: Dio portrays them, like the Caledonians, as living in tents, holding wives in common and fighting from chariots, a stereotype of barbarians rather than a reliable description. Around 197 the governor Virius Lupus had to buy peace from them with large sums of money. The hill names Dumyat and Myot Hill near Stirling are thought to preserve their name.
maeatae.e: Renewed raids brought Septimius Severus to Britain, and from 208 to 211 he campaigned against the Maeatae and Caledonii. The Maeatae revolted again in 210. After Severus died at York, Rome withdrew, and by about 300 the northern peoples were known as Picts, later forming the Kingdom of the Picts.

mandatory-palestine.t: The British-ruled mandate territory of Palestine, where the conflict between Jewish and Arab national movements took shape.
mandatory-palestine.o: After the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration, Britain set up a civil government under Herbert Samuel in July 1920. The League of Nations mandate, approved in 1922, incorporated the 1917 Balfour Declaration's promise of a Jewish national home, while Transjordan was administered separately.
mandatory-palestine.r: A high commissioner ruled without an elected legislature. Jewish immigration, land purchase and institutions such as the Jewish Agency and the Histadrut built the Yishuv, while Arab leaders opposed the national home. Violence erupted in 1920, 1921 and 1929, and the Arab revolt of 1936-1939 led the Peel Commission to propose partition. The 1939 White Paper limited Jewish immigration, and after 1944 Jewish groups fought the British.
mandatory-palestine.e: Britain referred the question to the United Nations, which approved partition in November 1947. The mandate ended on 14-15 May 1948, when the State of Israel was declared and war with Arab states followed.

moab.t: Moab, a kingdom east of the Dead Sea whose king Mesha recorded his revolt against Israel on the famous Mesha Stele.
moab.o: Moab took shape in the Iron Age on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, between the Arnon and Zered gorges. Egyptian texts mention the land in the 13th century BCE, and by the 9th century BCE it was a kingdom with its capital at Dibon.
moab.r: Moabite kings ruled a land of wheat fields and sheep pastures under the protection of the god Chemosh. The Mesha Stele, found at Dhiban in 1868, tells how Mesha freed Moab from the Kingdom of Israel after Ahab's dynasty had held it, building towns and reservoirs. Its language was close to Hebrew.
moab.e: Moab became a vassal of the Assyrian Empire in the 8th century BCE and later of the Chaldean Empire. A Babylonian campaign in 582 BCE ended its independence, and Arab tribes and later the Nabataean Kingdom took over the region.

marquisate-of-finale.t: A small Ligurian marquisate of the Del Carretto family whose port became Spain's private gateway to the Duchy of Milan.
marquisate-of-finale.o: In 1162 Frederick Barbarossa confirmed the rights of Enrico il Guercio, a member of the Aleramici family, over lands in western Liguria, including Finale. His descendants, the Del Carretto, made Finalborgo their seat.
marquisate-of-finale.r: The marquises ruled a small coastal and hill territory from the walled town of Finalborgo and the castle of Govone. They were repeatedly at war with the Republic of Genoa, which wanted to control the whole Ligurian coast; Genoa occupied Finale in 1447–1448 and again in the 16th century. The Del Carretto relied on imperial and Spanish protection, as Finale offered a landing place outside Genoese control.
marquisate-of-finale.e: The last marquis sold his rights to Spain, which took possession in 1602, and Finale served Habsburg Spain as a port for troops bound for Milan. In 1713 Emperor Charles VI sold it to Genoa.

march-of-tuscany.t: The great march of Tuscany, ruled from Lucca and later by the house of Canossa, whose Countess Matilda backed the papacy against the emperor.
march-of-tuscany.o: The Carolingians governed Tuscany through counts at Lucca. In 846 Adalbert I, of the Bonifacian family, succeeded his father and gathered the counties of Tuscany into a march, with the duty of defending the coast against Arab raids. His son Adalbert II, called the Rich, made the margraves among the most powerful lords in Italy.
march-of-tuscany.r: The margraves ruled a vast territory from Lucca, with influence in Rome and over the Italian crown. Hugh the Great, who died in 1001, founded the Badia of Florence. From 1027 the house of Canossa held the march; Countess Matilda (ruled 1076–1115) hosted the meeting at Canossa in 1077 where Emperor Henry IV sought Pope Gregory VII's forgiveness, and fought for the papacy for decades.
march-of-tuscany.e: After Matilda died in 1115, her will, leaving her lands to the Church, set pope against emperor. Imperial legates governed the march while the cities of Florence, Pisa, Lucca and Siena grew into self-governing communes. After Emperor Henry VI died in 1197 the Tuscan cities formed the League of San Genesio, ending the march.

miletus.t: The greatest Ionian city, mother of some ninety colonies around the Black Sea and birthplace of Greek natural philosophy with Thales and Anaximander.
miletus.o: After the Bronze Age town of Millawanda was destroyed, Ionian Greeks settled Miletus near the mouth of the Maeander c. 1000 BCE; tradition named Neleus, son of Codrus of Athens, as founder. By the 7th century BCE it was a wealthy trading city and a leading member of the Ionian League.
miletus.r: Miletus founded colonies such as Sinope, Cyzicus, Histria and Apollonia Pontica, and traded at Naucratis in Egypt. Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes worked there in the 6th century BCE. Tyrants such as Thrasybulus alternated with oligarchic factions. Miletus came under the Kingdom of Lydia and then the Achaemenid Empire, and its tyrants Histiaeus and Aristagoras launched the Ionian Revolt in 499 BCE.
miletus.e: Persia sacked the city in 494 BCE after the Battle of Lade. Rebuilt on a grid plan associated with Hippodamus, it joined the Delian League and was taken by Alexander in 334 BCE. After Hellenistic rule it passed to Rome in 133 BCE as part of the province of Asia.
miletus.re: Greek religion; oracle of Apollo at Didyma

margraviate-of-meissen.t: The Wettin march on the middle Elbe whose silver mines and rulers laid the foundations of the later Electorate and Kingdom of Saxony.
margraviate-of-meissen.o: After the death of Margrave Gero in 965, Otto I created a march around the stronghold of Meissen, founded by Henry the Fowler in 929 among the Sorbs. A bishopric followed in 968. From 1089 the march was held by the Wettin family, who kept it for more than eight centuries in its successor states.
margraviate-of-meissen.r: The Wettins promoted German settlement among the Sorbs and founded towns such as Leipzig and Dresden. The discovery of silver at Freiberg around 1168 made the margraves wealthy; Otto the Rich used it to fortify his lands. Henry the Illustrious added the Landgraviate of Thuringia in 1264, making the Wettins a leading princely house.
margraviate-of-meissen.e: In 1423 Emperor Sigismund granted Frederick the Warlike the Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg with its electoral dignity, after the Ascanian line died out. The margraviate merged into the Electorate of Saxony, and the name Saxony moved up the Elbe to the old lands of Meissen.

mac-william-iochtar.t: The Gaelicised Burke lordship of Mayo, ruled by the Lower Mac William, whose title survived until the late Tudor conquest of Connacht.
mac-william-iochtar.o: After the murder of the last Earl of Ulster in 1333, Edmund Albanach de Burgh took control of the de Burgh lands in north Connacht and adopted the Gaelic title Mac William Iochtar, the Lower Mac William. His descendants ruled much of modern Mayo.
mac-william-iochtar.r: The Mayo Burkes lived as Gaelic lords, electing their chief by tanistry, employing gallowglasses and poets, and allying with or fighting the O'Donnells, O'Malleys and the Clanricarde Burkes. Richard an Iarainn Burke, 'Iron Dick', married Grace O'Malley.
mac-william-iochtar.e: Under the Composition of Connacht in 1585 the title was abolished, and Mayo was shired. After Burke rebellions, Theobald Burke, 'Tibbot na Long', son of Grace O'Malley, sided with the crown and was made Viscount Mayo in 1627.

menteshe.t: A Turkish beylik on the Carian coast of south-western Anatolia, known for its naval raids into the Aegean.
menteshe.o: In the 1260s and 1270s Turkmen raiders led by Menteshe Bey occupied the Byzantine coastlands of Caria around Milas, Pecin and Miletus (Balat), founding one of the first maritime beyliks.
menteshe.r: The Menteshe rulers raided the Aegean islands, clashing with the Knights Hospitaller of Rhodes and Venice, but also traded with Italian merchants in Balat. Ibn Battuta visited Milas in the 1330s and praised its ruler Orhan Bey. Ilyas Bey built the mosque of Balat in 1404 next to the ruins of Miletus. Treaties with Venice and Crete regulated trade in grain, horses and slaves, and Turkish sailors from Menteshe ports joined the Aydinids in raids on the islands.
menteshe.e: Bayezid I annexed the beylik in 1390. Timur restored it after defeating Bayezid in 1402, but the Ottomans took it back for good in 1424.

magan.t: The copper land of south-eastern Arabia, known to Mesopotamian kings as the source of metal and hard stone shipped up the Gulf.
magan.o: Magan appears in cuneiform texts from the 23rd century BCE, when Sargon of Akkad boasted that ships from Magan, Meluhha and Dilmun moored at his capital. The name covered the copper-bearing Hajar Mountains of modern Oman and the United Arab Emirates, home of the Umm an-Nar culture with its round stone tombs and towers such as those at Hili and Bat.
magan.r: Little is known of its politics. Naram-Sin of the Akkadian Empire claimed to have defeated Manium, lord of Magan, and brought back diorite for statues. Magan exported copper, diorite and timber in Magan-boats, and later Ur III texts record merchants trading wool, textiles and oil for its copper. Whether it was ever a single kingdom or a federation of oasis communities is unclear.
magan.e: References fade after the early 2nd millennium BCE as Dilmun took over the copper trade. The name revived in Assyrian records and as Maka, a land listed among the subjects of the Achaemenid Empire in the 6th century BCE. Its copper mines and tombs remain the main witnesses to the Bronze Age of Oman.

marajoara.t: Mound-building chiefdoms on Marajó Island at the mouth of the Amazon, whose elaborate painted funerary urns show that complex societies flourished in Amazonia.
marajoara.o: From around 400 CE people on the eastern part of Marajó Island, in the Amazon delta of Brazil, began raising large earthen mounds called tesos above the seasonally flooded savannas. The Marajoara phase grew from earlier local pottery traditions and lasted roughly a thousand years.
marajoara.r: The largest mounds, such as Camutins and Os Pacoval, held houses, cemeteries and ceremonial spaces, and some supported thousands of people. Society was probably organised in ranked chiefdoms. The economy relied on fish managed in ponds and channels, palm fruits and root crops rather than intensive maize farming. Marajoara potters made polychrome burial urns, figurines and ceramic tangas, small triangular pubic covers, decorated with incised and painted designs, many with female imagery.
marajoara.e: Mound building ceased around 1400, before European arrival, possibly because of social change or new groups entering the island. Marajoara urns are prized museum pieces and inspired modern Brazilian decorative styles. The culture is central to debates over how many people lived in pre-Columbian Amazonia.

marquisate-of-saluzzo.t: An Alpine marquisate in south-western Piedmont that balanced between Savoy, France and the Dauphiné for four centuries.
marquisate-of-saluzzo.o: The marquisate was formed in 1142 when the lands of Boniface del Vasto were divided among his sons, and Manfred I received Saluzzo and the upper valleys of the Po, Varaita and Maira.
marquisate-of-saluzzo.r: The marquises ruled from their castle at Saluzzo over a small state of mountain valleys and plain. Squeezed between the County of Savoy and the Dauphiné, they often sought French protection. Marquis Thomas III wrote the allegorical romance Le Chevalier errant around 1400. Ludovico II opened the Buco di Viso tunnel under the Alps around 1480 to trade salt and goods with Provence, and the town flourished as a small Renaissance court.
marquisate-of-saluzzo.e: After quarrels in the ruling family, King Henry II of France annexed the marquisate in 1548. It was occupied by Charles Emmanuel I of the Duchy of Savoy in 1588 and formally ceded to Savoy by the Treaty of Lyon in 1601.

mytilene.t: Chief city of Lesbos, home of the poets Sappho and Alcaeus, whose revolt against Athens in 428 BCE prompted the famous Mytilenean Debate.
mytilene.o: Aeolian Greeks settled Lesbos around 1000 BCE, and Mytilene grew on the south-east coast of the island, with harbours facing Anatolia. By the 7th century BCE it was the leading city of Lesbos, founding settlements in the Troad and fighting Athens for Sigeion.
mytilene.r: Aristocratic feuds and tyrants such as Myrsilus marked the 7th century BCE, ended when Pittacus, one of the Seven Sages, ruled as elected aesymnetes c. 590 to 580 BCE. Sappho and Alcaeus wrote lyric poetry there. Mytilene shared in the Greek trading post at Naucratis, and later belonged to the Delian League as a ship-providing ally.
mytilene.e: After its revolt of 428 BCE Athens first voted to kill all its men, then relented. Mytilene sided with Mithridates of the Kingdom of Pontus, and its capture by Rome in 79 BCE, where the young Julius Caesar won the civic crown, ended its independence, though Pompey later granted it freedom.

maona-of-chios.t: Genoese chartered company that ruled Chios for over two centuries and grew rich on the island's unique mastic monopoly.
maona-of-chios.o: In 1346 a Genoese fleet under Simone Vignoso, financed by private shareholders, seized Chios from the Byzantines and also Old and New Phocaea on the Anatolian coast. Genoa, unable to repay the investors, let them govern and exploit the island through a company, the maona, whose members took the shared surname Giustiniani.
maona-of-chios.r: The maona appointed a podesta and council, collected taxes and controlled the export of mastic, a resin produced only in southern Chios and prized as a chewing gum and medicine, as well as alum and silk. The Greek Orthodox population kept its church and grew prosperous through trade. From the early 15th century the maona paid tribute to the Ottomans.
maona-of-chios.e: In 1566 the Ottoman admiral Piyale Pasha occupied Chios without a fight, ending Genoese rule. Many Giustiniani were deported, while the mastic villages kept special privileges under the Ottomans.

mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate.t: An autonomous Ottoman district of Mount Lebanon under a Christian governor and European guarantee, the core of the later Lebanese state.
mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate.o: After the 1860 civil war, the Ottoman government and five European powers agreed in 1861 a Reglement Organique that united Mount Lebanon as a single autonomous district. It was governed by a non-Lebanese Ottoman Catholic mutasarrif appointed with the powers' consent.
mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate.r: The first mutasarrif was Daud Pasha, an Armenian Catholic. An administrative council represented the religious communities in proportion, an early form of Lebanon's confessional system. Feudal privileges were abolished and the mountain enjoyed decades of peace. Silk production for French mills flourished, schools multiplied and emigration to the Americas grew. The district lacked Beirut and the Beqaa, which remained in Ottoman provinces.
mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate.e: In 1915 Jamal Pasha ended the autonomy; wartime blockade and famine killed a large part of the population. French troops arrived in 1918, and in 1920 the mountain became the heart of Greater Lebanon.

monarchy-of-the-north.t: A royalist counter-revolution that restored the monarchy in northern Portugal for less than a month in 1919.
monarchy-of-the-north.o: After the assassination of the dictator Sidónio Pais in December 1918, royalists saw an opportunity to overthrow the First Portuguese Republic. On 19 January 1919 Henrique Paiva Couceiro proclaimed the monarchy in Porto in the name of the exiled Manuel II.
monarchy-of-the-north.r: A royal governing junta ruled Porto and much of the north, restored the blue-and-white monarchist flag and the Charter of 1826. Manuel II, in exile in England, did not endorse the rising. A parallel royalist rising near Lisbon, at Monsanto, was quickly defeated.
monarchy-of-the-north.e: Republican forces, supported by armed civilians, advanced north, and a republican revolt in Porto on 13 February 1919 ended the royalist regime. Paiva Couceiro fled to Galicia. It was the last serious attempt to restore the Portuguese monarchy.

margraviate-of-moravia.t: Land of the Bohemian Crown with Brno and Olomouc as its centres, a margraviate for over seven centuries until the end of Austria-Hungary.
margraviate-of-moravia.o: Moravia had been the core of Great Moravia and was later ruled by Přemyslid princes as appanages of Bohemia. In 1182 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa named Conrad III Otto margrave, briefly making Moravia a direct imperial fief. It soon returned under Bohemian kings, remaining a distinct land with its own estates, diet and law.
margraviate-of-moravia.r: Margraves were usually members or appointees of the Bohemian royal house, among them the future Charles IV and Jobst of Moravia, who was elected King of the Romans in 1410. Brno and Olomouc competed as capitals. Czech and German were spoken, and Moravia sheltered the Unity of the Brethren, whose Kralice Bible shaped written Czech. After 1620 Habsburg rule enforced Catholicism, and Brno later became a textile centre.
margraviate-of-moravia.e: Moravia remained a crown land of the Habsburg Monarchy, Austrian Empire and Austria-Hungary until 1918, when it joined Czechoslovakia. It was merged with Czech Silesia in 1928 and abolished as a unit in 1949; it now forms the eastern Czech Republic.

methymna.t: Second city of Lesbos, rival of Mytilene, birthplace of the legendary singer Arion and a loyal ally of Athens.
methymna.o: Methymna was founded by Aeolian settlers on the north coast of Lesbos c. 1000 BCE, on a headland facing the Troad. It grew into the second city of the island and a long-standing rival of Mytilene for control of Lesbos.
methymna.r: Methymna was governed mostly by aristocracies and oligarchies. Herodotus tells how the singer Arion of Methymna was saved by a dolphin. In 428 BCE it refused to join Mytilene's revolt and remained an autonomous ship-providing ally in the Delian League, later joining the Second Athenian League. The city was famed for its wine.
methymna.e: Methymna came under Hellenistic kings and in the 2nd century BCE became an ally of Rome. It was included in the Roman province of Asia from 129 BCE. The town survives as modern Mithymna, also called Molyvos.
