margraviate-of-hachberg.t: Breisgau branch of the margraves of Baden, named after the Hachberg castle and later holding Rötteln, Sausenberg and Neuchâtel before reuniting with Baden in 1503.
margraviate-of-hachberg.o: Around 1190 the lands of Margrave Hermann IV of Baden were divided, and his son Henry received the castle of Hachberg, the Hochburg near Emmendingen, with lands in the Breisgau. Henry and his heirs styled themselves margraves of Hachberg, founding a separate branch of the house of Zähringen-Baden.
margraviate-of-hachberg.r: The margraves held scattered lordships in the Breisgau and Markgräflerland. In 1306 the house split into Hachberg proper and Hachberg-Sausenberg, which gained Rötteln in 1315 and, through marriage, the County of Neuchâtel in the 15th century. Hachberg proper was sold back to Baden in 1415. Philip of Hachberg-Sausenberg served the dukes of Burgundy and the French crown.
margraviate-of-hachberg.e: Philip died in 1503 without a son, and under an inheritance treaty his lands returned to the margraves of Baden, while Neuchâtel passed through his daughter to the Orléans-Longueville family. The Markgräflerland name recalls their rule.

morini.t: Coastal people of the Pas-de-Calais, called by Virgil the farthest of men, from whose harbour Caesar sailed to invade Britain.
morini.o: The Morini, whose name means people of the sea, lived along the Channel coast from the Somme to the Scheldt, in a land of dunes, marshes and forest. They joined the Belgic coalition of 57 BCE.
morini.r: They lived by farming, herding and salt-making, and took refuge in forests and marshes rather than defending oppida. Their coast was the shortest crossing to Britain.
morini.e: Caesar campaigned against them in 56 and 55 BCE and sailed for Britain from Portus Itius in their land, probably Boulogne. Under Rome their capital was Tarvenna (Thérouanne), while Gesoriacum (Boulogne) became the base of the Roman Channel fleet.

mahdid-dynasty.t: A puritanical reformist dynasty that seized Zabid in 1159 and ruled the Yemeni Tihama until the Ayyubid invasion.
mahdid-dynasty.o: Ali ibn Mahdi, a preacher from the Tihama, built a following among the tribes of the coastal plain in the 1130s and 1140s, preaching strict morality and condemning the ruling elite. After years of raids he captured Zabid in 1159, ending the Najahid dynasty, and died soon after.
mahdid-dynasty.r: His sons, especially Abd al-Nabi, ran a militant state. Contemporary sources, mostly hostile, accuse them of treating other Muslims as unbelievers, punishing minor sins with death and destroying tombs. They raided widely across the Tihama and threatened Aden, ruled by the Zurayid dynasty.
mahdid-dynasty.e: In 1174 the Ayyubid prince Turan-Shah, sent by his brother Saladin, invaded Yemen, took Zabid and executed Abd al-Nabi, absorbing the Mahdid lands into Ayyubid Yemen.

millawanda.t: Bronze Age Miletus as named in Hittite texts, a coastal foothold of the Aegean Ahhiyawa on the Anatolian mainland and a flashpoint with the Hittites.
millawanda.o: Excavations at Miletus show a Minoan-style settlement from c. 1900 BCE, followed after c. 1450 BCE by a town with Mycenaean pottery, tombs and customs. Most scholars identify this town with Millawanda, or Milawata, named in Hittite sources as a place under the influence of Ahhiyawa, the power of the Mycenaean Greeks.
millawanda.r: The Tawagalawa letter of Hattusili III, c. 1250 BCE, names Atpa as the local ruler, son-in-law of the rebel Piyamaradu, who used Millawanda as a base for raids on Hittite lands. The town was a port linking the Aegean with western Anatolia, and the Hittite Mursili II had sacked it c. 1315 BCE during his wars with Arzawa.
millawanda.e: The so-called Milawata letter, probably from Tudhaliya IV, shows the town had passed under Hittite control and a new border was being fixed. Miletus was destroyed c. 1200 BCE, then resettled by Ionian Greeks as the city-state Miletus.

mycenaean-kingdom-of-laconia.t: Mycenaean palace state of the Eurotas valley, the Bronze Age Sparta of Homer's Menelaus, recently revealed by the palace and tablets of Ayios Vasileios.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-laconia.o: In the Eurotas valley of Laconia, Mycenaean elites appear from c. 1500 BCE, as shown by the rich tholos tomb of Vapheio with its gold cups. A palace was built at Ayios Vasileios, about 12 kilometres south of Sparta, while the Menelaion at Therapne, opposite the later city, held a large mansion.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-laconia.r: Excavations at Ayios Vasileios since 2008 have found a palace with a large court, stoas, wall paintings and the first Linear B tablets from Laconia, recording textiles, personnel and offerings. Laconia also produced the green porphyry stone from Krokeai, exported across the Aegean. The kingdom presumably ruled the Eurotas plain.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-laconia.e: The Ayios Vasileios palace was destroyed by fire well before the general collapse, and the Menelaion buildings were abandoned c. 1200 BCE. Laconia was largely depopulated afterwards, and Dorian Sparta later grew nearby. Homer remembered Laconia as the kingdom of Menelaus and Helen.

mamertine-messana.t: Messana under the Mamertines, Campanian mercenaries whose appeals to both Carthage and Rome set off the First Punic War in 264 BCE.
mamertine-messana.o: The Mamertines were Campanian mercenaries who had served Agathocles of Syracuse. After his death they seized Messana by treachery around 288 BCE, killing or expelling many of the men and taking their property. They called themselves Mamertini, 'sons of Mamers', the Oscan war god.
mamertine-messana.r: From Messana the Mamertines raided and taxed much of north-eastern Sicily, ruling as a military community with Oscan magistrates; their coins name them in Greek. Their power was broken by Hieron II of Syracuse, who defeated them at the Longanus river in the 260s BCE. Facing capture, one faction called in a Carthaginian garrison while another appealed to Rome.
mamertine-messana.e: Rome's decision to send an army to Messana in 264 BCE began the First Punic War. Messana became an ally of Rome, and after the war in 241 BCE it was a privileged allied city in Roman Sicily, today Messina.

marca-geronis.t: The vast eastern march of Margrave Gero, from which Otto I's frontier against the Slavs between the Elbe and the Oder was controlled.
marca-geronis.o: In 937 Otto I appointed Gero as margrave on the eastern frontier of Saxony, over the Slavic lands between the Saale and the Elbe and beyond. Gero extended German control in campaigns against the Hevelli, the Lusatians and other Slavs. Widukind of Corvey reports that he killed some thirty Slavic chiefs at a banquet.
marca-geronis.r: The march was a military command over tribute-paying Slavic peoples, the Sorbs among them, rather than a settled principality. Gero campaigned as far as the Oder and in 963 forced the Polish ruler Mieszko I to pay tribute for land up to the Warta. He founded the convent of Gernrode, where he was buried.
marca-geronis.e: When Gero died in 965 Otto I divided his march into smaller units: the Northern March, the Margraviate of Meissen, the March of Lusatia (later Margraviate of Lower Lusatia), and the marches of Merseburg and Zeitz. Bishoprics founded in 968 under the Archbishopric of Magdeburg completed the new frontier order.

montenegro.t: Present-day Montenegro, independent again since 2006 after nearly nine decades within Yugoslav states, and a NATO member seeking to join the EU.
montenegro.o: Under Milo Đukanović, Montenegro distanced itself from Serbia in the late 1990s and adopted the Deutsche Mark and later the euro. Within Serbia and Montenegro, it used its right to hold an independence referendum, and on 21 May 2006 a narrow majority voted to leave. Independence was declared on 3 June 2006, restoring the statehood lost in 1918 by the Kingdom of Montenegro.
montenegro.r: Montenegro is a parliamentary republic with its capital at Podgorica, while Cetinje, the old royal capital, keeps the official residence of the president. A constitution adopted in 2007 made Montenegrin the official language. Đukanović's Democratic Party of Socialists dominated politics for three decades, and tourism along the Adriatic coast is the mainstay of the economy.
montenegro.e: Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 despite Russian opposition and an alleged coup plot in 2016. A dispute over a law on church property brought the opposition to power in 2020, ending thirty years of rule by the Democratic Party of Socialists. It is among the most advanced candidates for EU membership.

middle-francia.t: Central share of the Carolingian empire, stretching from Frisia to Rome, given to the emperor Lothair I in 843.
middle-francia.o: The Treaty of Verdun in 843 ended the war between the sons of Louis the Pious. The eldest, Lothair I, kept the imperial title and received a long strip of land between West Francia and East Francia, including the imperial cities of Aachen and Rome.
middle-francia.r: The kingdom reached from the North Sea through the Low Countries, the Rhineland, Burgundy and Provence to Italy. It held the richest heartlands of the Carolingian dynasty but had no common identity, language or natural frontiers, and suffered Viking attacks in Frisia and Arab raids in the south.
middle-francia.e: Shortly before his death in 855 Lothair retired to the abbey of Prüm and, by the Treaty of Prüm, divided the kingdom among his three sons: Louis II received Italy, Lothair II the north, which became the Kingdom of Lotharingia, and Charles the Kingdom of Provence.

mediomatrici.t: Gallic people of the Moselle valley whose chief town Divodurum became the city of Metz.
mediomatrici.o: The Mediomatrici held the middle Moselle and Seille valleys in Lorraine. Caesar notes that their territory once reached the Rhine, before Germanic peoples such as the Triboci settled on its left bank.
mediomatrici.r: Little is known of their rulers. Their territory lay on the trade routes linking the Rhône and Saône with the Rhine and the Moselle, and their oppidum at Divodurum controlled the Moselle crossing.
mediomatrici.e: They sent five thousand men to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE. Under Rome Divodurum became a major town on the road from Lyon to Trier, known in late antiquity as Mettis after the people, from which comes Metz, later capital of Austrasia.

megara.t: City-state on the Isthmus between Athens and Corinth that founded Byzantium and Chalcedon and whose trade ban by Athens helped spark the Peloponnesian War.
megara.o: Megara occupied the small plain of the Megarid between Attica and Corinth. Dorian settlers formed the city in the early Iron Age, and it may once have been subject to Corinth before becoming independent. Its limited farmland pushed it to the sea, and from the 8th century BCE it founded colonies.
megara.r: Megarians founded Megara Hyblaea in Sicily, Chalcedon, Byzantium and later Heraclea Pontica. Theagenes ruled as tyrant c. 640 BCE and backed his son-in-law Cylon's failed coup at Athens. Megara lost the island of Salamis to Athens in the 6th century BCE. The poet Theognis and the philosopher Euclid of Megara were citizens. It belonged to the Peloponnesian League.
megara.e: The Megarian Decree of c. 432 BCE barred it from Athenian markets and helped start the Peloponnesian War. Megara joined the Achaean League in 243 BCE and passed under Roman control in 146 BCE.

marquisate-of-bodonitsa.t: Frankish frontier march guarding the pass of Thermopylae, which outlived most crusader states in Greece until the Ottomans took it in 1414.
marquisate-of-bodonitsa.o: In 1204 Boniface of Montferrat granted the strategic castle of Bodonitsa, above the Thermopylae pass, to the Italian knight Guido Pallavicini. The marquisate was intended as a buffer protecting the Frankish lands of southern Greece from attack from the north.
marquisate-of-bodonitsa.r: Bodonitsa was a small feudal state centred on its hill fortress, whose ruins still stand. Its marquesses were vassals first of the Kingdom of Thessalonica and later of the Principality of Achaea, with some ties to the Latin Empire. The Pallavicini line was followed in 1335 by the Venetian Zorzi family through marriage, which brought Venetian protection.
marquisate-of-bodonitsa.e: Catalan, Byzantine and Turkish pressure reduced the marquisate. The Ottomans briefly took it in 1393 and finally captured Bodonitsa in 1414, ending the state. The Zorzi kept the title and the island of Aegina for some years.

mycenaean-kingdom-of-orchomenos.t: Rich Mycenaean centre of Boeotia, home of the legendary Minyans, which drained Lake Copais in one of the great engineering feats of the Bronze Age.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-orchomenos.o: Orchomenos, on the north-west edge of Lake Copais in Boeotia, was an important settlement from the Early Bronze Age and gave its name to the grey 'Minyan ware' pottery. By c. 1600 BCE it was home to a Mycenaean elite, and its wealth later became proverbial: Homer compared it with Egyptian Thebes.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-orchomenos.r: The so-called Treasury of Minyas, a great tholos tomb with a carved stone ceiling, shows the power of its rulers in the 13th century BCE. Remains of a palace with frescoes have been found. Orchomenos is usually credited with draining the Copais basin by dykes and canals, protected by the huge fortress of Gla, creating rich farmland and rivalling Thebes.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-orchomenos.e: The drainage works and Gla were abandoned c. 1200 BCE, when the lake flooded again, and the palace system collapsed. Orchomenos survived as a Boeotian city, later a rival of Thebes within the Boeotian League, and is described separately as Orchomenus (Boeotia).

margraviate-of-styria.t: The Carantanian March on the Mur that grew into Styria, elevated to a duchy in 1180 and later inherited by the Babenbergs and Habsburgs.
margraviate-of-styria.o: The Carantanian March arose around 970 on the south-eastern border of the Duchy of Carinthia, along the Mur, as a frontier against the Magyars. From 1056 it was ruled by the Otakar family of Steyr, and the territory took its name, Styria (Steiermark), from their castle of Steyr in Upper Austria.
margraviate-of-styria.r: The Otakar margraves gradually made the march independent of Carinthia, adding lands around Graz and in the Enns valley. They founded monasteries such as Admont and Rein and encouraged colonisation of the hill country. Iron mining at the Erzberg near Eisenerz became a lasting source of wealth.
margraviate-of-styria.e: In 1180 Frederick Barbarossa raised Styria to a duchy under Ottokar IV. Having no heir, he concluded the Georgenberg Pact in 1186, leaving Styria to the Babenberg dukes of Austria, who inherited in 1192. Styria remained part of the Habsburg lands until 1918.

marwanids.t: A Kurdish dynasty that ruled Diyar Bakr from Mayyafariqin and Amid, with a long, prosperous reign under Nasr al-Dawla in the 11th century.
marwanids.o: In the 980s the Kurdish chief Badh took advantage of Buyid weakness to seize Mayyafariqin, Amid and much of Diyar Bakr. After his death in 990 his nephew Abu Ali ibn Marwan took over the domain, founding the dynasty that bears his father's name.
marwanids.r: Nasr al-Dawla Ahmad ibn Marwan ruled for about fifty years (1011-1061), keeping peace with Byzantium, the Fatimids and the Seljuks by diplomacy and gifts. His capital Mayyafariqin gained mosques, a hospital, bridges and an observatory, and attracted scholars, including the vizier Ibn Jahir and refugees from Baghdad. The population mixed Kurds, Arabs, Armenians and Syriac Christians, and the dynasty was Sunni.
marwanids.e: After Nasr al-Dawla's death the emirate became a Seljuk vassal. Around 1085 Malik-Shah sent its former vizier Fakhr al-Dawla ibn Jahir to conquer it, and Diyar Bakr passed to Seljuk governors and later to the Inalids and Artuqids.

mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes.t: Mycenaean palace kingdom on the Kadmeia hill in Boeotia, whose Linear B archive and Near Eastern treasures mark it as one of the major Bronze Age Greek powers.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes.o: Thebes occupies the Kadmeia, a low plateau between fertile plains in southern Boeotia. A palace centre emerged there by c. 1600 BCE, and by the 14th century BCE its rulers controlled much of Boeotia and perhaps Euboea. Greek myth gave the citadel its name from Cadmus, its legendary Phoenician founder.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes.r: Excavations under the modern town have uncovered parts of the palace, workshops for jewellery and ivory, and a hoard of Near Eastern cylinder seals of lapis lazuli. Several hundred Linear B tablets record offerings to gods, wool, food rations and places as far as Euboea. Some scholars argue that Thebes was the centre of the Ahhiyawa named in Hittite texts.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes.e: The palace was destroyed by fire in the 13th century BCE, the setting later remembered in the myths of Oedipus and the Seven against Thebes. The city remained inhabited and became the leading Boeotian city-state, described separately as Thebes.

massalia.t: Greek colony at Marseille, the oldest city in France, through which Greek wine, coinage and writing reached the peoples of Gaul for five centuries.
massalia.o: Settlers from Phocaea in Asia Minor founded the city around 600 BCE on the sheltered harbour of the Lacydon, east of the Rhône delta. Tradition says their leader Protis married Gyptis, daughter of Nannus, king of the local Segobrigii. Refugees arrived after Phocaea fell to Persia in 545 BCE, and Massalia planted daughter towns such as Nikaia (Nice), Antipolis (Antibes) and Emporion in Spain.
massalia.r: The city was an aristocratic republic governed by a council of six hundred timouchoi, praised by Aristotle and Strabo for its stability. It traded wine, oil and fine pottery up the Rhône for tin, metals and slaves, and its silver coins were widely copied by Gallic peoples. Artemis of Ephesus and Apollo Delphinios were its chief cults, and around 325 BCE its navigator Pytheas sailed to Britain and the North Sea.
massalia.e: A steady ally of the Roman Republic, Massalia called in Roman armies against the Salyes from 125 BCE, opening the way to the province of Gallia Narbonensis. Having sided with Pompey, it was besieged and taken by Caesar's forces in 49 BCE and lost its fleet and most of its territory, yet it lived on as a free Greek city under the Roman Empire.

marrucini.t: Small Sabellic people on the Adriatic coast around Teate (Chieti), allies of Rome from 304 BCE and rebels in the Social War.
marrucini.o: The Marrucini occupied a narrow strip between the Aterno river and the Foro, inland of the Adriatic coast in modern Abruzzo, with Teate as their main town. They were counted among the Sabellian peoples and spoke a dialect close to Oscan.
marrucini.r: Little is known of their organisation beyond a single community centred on Teate. A bronze inscription from Rapino, the Tabula Rapinensis, records a sacred regulation in their dialect. Like their neighbours, they lived by farming and herding.
marrucini.e: The Marrucini made an alliance with Rome in 304 BCE with the Marsi and Paeligni and fought for Rome against Hannibal. In the Social War they joined the rebels; their commander Herius Asinius was killed in 90 BCE. They gained citizenship afterwards, and Teate became a Roman municipium.

marsi.t: Warlike Sabellic people of the Fucine Lake basin, famed as snake charmers, who led the Italian revolt against Rome in 91 BCE.
marsi.o: The Marsi lived around the Fucine Lake in the central Apennines of Abruzzo from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers linked their name to Marsyas or to Mars and considered them part of the Sabellian peoples. They spoke Marsian, an Italic dialect related to Umbrian and Oscan.
marsi.r: Their main centre was Marruvium on the lake shore. Romans regarded the Marsi as experts in magic, healing and snake-charming, linked to the goddess Angitia, whose grove stood by the lake. They were renowned as soldiers; a Roman saying held that no one had ever triumphed over the Marsi or without them. They lived from farming, fishing and herding.
marsi.e: The Marsi allied with Rome in 304 BCE and served loyally for two centuries. In 91 BCE, led by Quintus Poppaedius Silo, they were among the first to rise in the Social War, sometimes called the Marsic War. They received citizenship afterwards, and the Fucine Lake was drained in the 19th century.

mantinea.t: Democratic Arcadian city that twice gave its name to great battles and was twice destroyed for opposing Sparta and Macedon.
mantinea.o: Mantinea grew from the union of several villages on the high plain of eastern Arcadia, a synoecism usually dated to around 500 BCE or soon after. Its constant rival was Tegea, which shared the same plain and its scarce water. Mantinea was normally a member of Sparta's Peloponnesian League but resented Spartan control.
mantinea.r: Unusually for Arcadia, Mantinea had a moderate democracy, admired by Aristotle, in which farmers voted but elected officials did the governing. It was famous for its well-drilled hoplites. In 418 BCE it joined Argos and Athens against Sparta and was defeated at the first Battle of Mantinea; in 385 BCE Sparta broke the city into villages by damming the river Ophis against its walls.
mantinea.e: Refounded in 370 BCE, Mantinea helped create the Arcadian League, and in 362 BCE Epaminondas died winning the second Battle of Mantinea. After it joined Cleomenes III of Sparta, the Achaean League and Antigonus Doson destroyed it in 223 BCE and renamed it Antigoneia. Hadrian later restored the old name.
